intro:
A good Halloween name tells you what kind of scary you're in for. A vampire wants an old title and a family name with history behind it. A ghost is usually named for the colour it wears or the place it haunts, like the Grey Ladies of English ghost stories. A zombie can be grim or downright silly, and a werewolf name often means "wolf" in an old language.

The Witch, Black Cat and Haunted House name generators cover costumes, pets and attractions. Use any of these for a costume character, a haunted house at the school fair, a one-shot for your gaming group or a spooky short story. For the party itself, the Event Name Generator has party names, and the Villain and Demon generators cover anything with horns or a cape.

For witches' gatherings there's the Coven and Spell name generators. For things that lurk, try Monster, Skeleton, Mummy and Scarecrow. And if you're writing the story yourself, the Horror Movie Title Generator will give it a name.

For a proper ghost-story night, the Local Legend Generator makes up British folk legends, the Haunted Pub generator gives every inn its ghost, and there are names for ghost hunting teams and paranormal podcasts.

If you'd like to spend Halloween somewhere with a ghost of its own, our sister site Haunted Hotels UK has haunted hotels to book for the night, with the famous rooms you can request.

Once the pumpkins are on the compost, the Christmas name generators take over, from Elf on the Shelf names to Christmas quiz teams.

approach.heading: How to approach Halloween names
approach.text: A good Halloween name tells people what kind of scary they're in for before they read another word. Britain's ghosts are named the way witnesses described them, by colour and by who they seemed to be, which is why so many old houses have a Grey Lady. Vampires borrow titles and old family names, haunted inns borrow the pattern of real pub signs, and costumes and pets suit a pun. Decide first whether you want a shiver or a grin, then pick the style that matches.

Name a ghost by its colour or its job.
Give a vampire a title and a family.

Elves suit a cosy first name, a festive surname and a workshop job. Snowmen suit whatever they're wearing. For quiz teams and family games, a pun on a carol or a cracker joke is all you need.

approach.heading: How to approach fantasy names
approach.text: The best fantasy names sound as if they belong to a language, even an invented one. Tolkien built his elves' names from languages he made up, and took most of his dwarves' names from the Old Norse poem the Völuspá, which is why they still sound right together. Decide how each people sounds before you name anyone: soft and flowing for elves, hard and blunt for dwarves and orcs, grand and ancient for dragons. Then keep to it, so a reader can tell where a character comes from before they're introduced.

approach.heading: How to approach world names
approach.text: Name a world from the outside in. Start with the world and its continents, then the kingdoms on them, then the mountains, rivers and forests that divide them, and the villages and dungeons in between. Each layer can borrow from the one above: a northern continent gives its rivers northern names, and a dwarven kingdom names its mountains in its own tongue. Real landscapes were named the same way, by whoever lived nearby, which is why a fell, a tor and a ben are all hills.

One language per region.
Fell in the north, tor in the south-west.

approach.heading: How to approach folklore names
approach.text: Folklore names are what people said around the fire, so they're plain and often careful. In Britain and Ireland, fairies were called the good folk or the fair folk, partly so as not to offend them. Ghosts were named for what witnesses saw: a colour, a job, a habit, like the many Grey Ladies of old houses. Werewolf names lean on the old word for wolf, which turns up in names like Wolfgang and the Old English wulf. Keep folklore names simple, local and a little uneasy, as if someone is still telling the story.

approach.heading: How to approach creature names
approach.text: Mythical creatures arrive with a history, and their names should respect it. Many of them come to us through Greek: the griffin from grups, the hydra from the word for a water snake. The ancient historian Herodotus wrote that the phoenix came to Heliopolis, the Egyptian city of the sun. A good creature name draws on the same roots or on what the creature does: fire for a phoenix, the sea for a kraken, gold and mountains for a griffin. Then decide whether it should be noble, frightening or friendly, and choose the style to match.

seoDescription: Elder Scrolls name generators for Skyrim and ESO: Nord, Khajiit, Dunmer, Altmer, Argonian and Orc names, each following that race's naming customs.
intro:
Every race in the Elder Scrolls names itself differently. Orcs add gro- or gra- and a parent's name; Khajiit wear prefixes like the J' in J'zargo; Nords have hyphenated family names like Battle-Born; Argonians may go by a description, like Scouts-Many-Marshes. These generators follow each race's customs, with examples from Skyrim, so your character sounds like they belong in Tamriel.

Each page explains how that race's names work. They suit Skyrim, Elder Scrolls Online, where names must be unique on your server, and tabletop games set in Tamriel.

approach.heading: How to approach Elder Scrolls names
approach.text: Each people in The Elder Scrolls names itself differently, so start with the race. Nords take Old Norse-style names and an epithet earned in battle. Khajiit names often carry an apostrophe prefix that says something about the bearer's standing. Argonians may be known by what they do, translated into a phrase like Wades-Through-Fog. Dark elves and high elves have long, formal names with their own sounds. Match the pattern, and an original name will fit in anywhere in Tamriel without borrowing anyone else's.

tips.heading: Quick tips
items: Start with the character's race.
Give Nords an earned epithet.
Use one Khajiit prefix, not two.
Let Argonians be named by deeds.
Avoid names from the games.

approach.heading: How to approach Warcraft names
approach.text: Warcraft's races each have a sound of their own, and a good name follows it. Orc names are short and hard, and a surname earned in battle or a clan says where loyalty lies. Night elf surnames come from the moon, the night and the forest. Blood elf names lean on the sun, fire and dawn. Trolls often use an apostrophe between two short sounds. Pick the race first, then the sound, and check the name is free on your realm before you make the character.

approach.heading: How to approach Warhammer names
approach.text: In Warhammer, a name is mostly a rank and a reputation. Space Marines put their title first and their Chapter last, so the name tells you who they are and who they answer to. Sisters of Battle carry saintly Latin-sounding names. Orks pile on titles and nicknames until the name runs out of breath, and Ogryns are known by a simple nickname, often in quotes. Decide the character's faction and rank first, then give them a name that sounds like the army they belong to.

Make it sound like the army.

approach.heading: How to approach sci-fi names
approach.text: A science fiction name should hint at the history between now and then. Colonists name new worlds after the places they left, so you get New Lagos or Upper Bristol. Navies name ships after virtues, and machines get serial numbers that people soften with nicknames. Real astronomy helps too: planets around other stars are labelled with the star's catalogue name and a lower-case letter, like 51 Pegasi b. Mix one familiar word with one strange one, and the future feels lived in rather than invented.

tips.heading: Quick tips
items: Give old Earth words a new home.
Use codes for machines, names for crews.
Let ships be named after virtues.
Keep alien names to one sound set.
Mix the familiar with the strange.

approach.heading: How to approach witch names
approach.text: Witch names in British folklore come from three places: plants, places and familiars. Village cunning folk were known by where they lived, hedge witches by the herbs they gathered, and the witch-finder Matthew Hopkins recorded familiars in the 1640s with names like Pyewacket. Fictional witches follow the same habits. Take a surname from a wild plant, add a title like Granny or Old Mother, and give the witch a familiar with a name of its own. For covens and spells, a moon, a place or a maker's name does the work.

tips.heading: Quick tips
items: Take a surname from a wild plant.
Give the witch a familiar with a name.
Name a coven after a moon or a place.
Put a maker's name on a spell.
Keep cosy witches cosy.

Romans had up to three names, Anglo-Saxons built names from two meaningful parts, and medieval English surnames came from jobs, places, fathers and nicknames. Pick the period first, then let the name follow its rules. A Roman with a modern surname, or a Saxon with a Norman first name, will jar with anyone who knows the period.
